content.text:
My recommendation is Piper as your default, with Kokoro as the upgrade if you want more natural voices and can spend some CPU. I'd skip XTTS on a laptop CPU.

Piper is built for CPU-only hardware, runs faster than real time even on a Raspberry Pi 4, and your project already pins and verifies its voices. The cost is that it sounds a bit more synthetic.

Kokoro, at 82 million parameters, sounds noticeably more natural and is Apache licensed. Its CPU speed is less certain: one benchmark showed about twice real time, while other sources claim faster on Apple chips. That is fine for sentence-by-sentence streaming but tighter than Piper.

XTTS v2 is the slowest, with reports from about 0.4 times real time up to a sentence every 30 seconds on CPU. Its weights are also non-commercial, so it only makes sense for voice cloning on a GPU.

One caveat: these numbers come from blogs and forum posts on unnamed hardware, and none compared all three directly. Before switching, run a quick real-time factor test of Kokoro on your own laptop, which the sources suggest is the only reliable check.

The sources were the Codesota speech synthesis guide, the Local AI Master and PromptQuorum local TTS guides, the Bittide Kokoro CPU benchmark post, and the Idiap coqui-tts documentation.
